name: Ayutla Mixe
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Romero-Méndez, Rodrigo. 2008 [©2009]. A Reference Grammar of Ayutla Mixe (Tukyo'm Ayuujk). PhD dissertation, University at Buffalo, SUNY. §3.7 'Stress', pp. 80-83. Convergent: Lyon, Don D. 1980. Mixe de Tlahuitoltepec, Oaxaca (Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas de México 8). México: CIIS / El Colegio de México. 'El acento', pp. 33-34.
catalog_quote: In Ayutla Mixe, there are two patterns for stress. Except in verbs, the stress is word final. In verbs, on the other hand, the last syllable of the verb stem is stressed. The verb stem is defined as what is left after the inflectional morphology is removed. ... In phonetic terms, the stress is usually realized as both higher pitch and greater intensity. In phonological terms, stress does not have any contrastive function, i.e. there are no minimal pairs with exactly the same segments in which the only difference resides in a different location of stress. ... In compounds, the last syllable of the second root takes the stress ... Prefixes do not interact with stress patterns. When a prefix is added, the root still bears the stress (125). ... inflectional suffixes do not take stress, as in (126). In the verb, it is possible to add one (127a), two (127b), and up to three syllables to the right of the root (127b), and in all of these cases the main stress will still be on the last syllable of the stem. [Romero-Méndez 2008:80-81] || Lyon 1980:33: En el sistema fonémico del mixe de Tlahuitoltepec el valor funcional del acento es mínimo. Hasta la fecha no hemos encontrado ningún ejemplo de contraste. Sin embargo, el acento es fonémico en tanto que no es posible predecir cuál sílaba de la palabra será la tónica. ... Con excepción de ciertos sufijos verbales que siempre son tónicos, la sílaba tónica de la palabra es la sílaba del radical.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked ( present, lists file->citation->URL for all four PDFs). (1) : extracted text of pp. 102-105 (printed pp. 80-83) shows section '3.7 Stress' opening exactly as quoted: 'In Ayutla Mixe, there are two patterns for stress. Except in verbs, the stress is word final. In verbs, on the other hand, the last syllable of the verb stem is stressed. In phonological terms, stress does not have any contrastive function, i.e. there are no mini…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the stem: in nouns, adjectives and other non-verbs (which have essentially no post-stem inflection) this is the word-final syllable; in verbs it is the final syllable of the verb stem, with all inflectional suffixes (inverse, plural, perfect, dependent markers) unstressed. Prefixes never affect stress; compounds stress the last syllable of the second root; enclitics are unstressed. Stress is non-contrastive, realized as higher pitch and greater intensity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In a trisyllabic word the first syllable takes secondary stress and the last primary (132); if the third syllable is a suffix, primary on the second and no secondary (133); when two or three suffix syllables follow the stem, the word-final syllable carries secondary stress while the stem-final syllable keeps primary (127, 134); with noun plural -tëjk the (stressed) suffix is preceded by a secondarily stressed penult (fn. 13). Author notes other Mixe languages show a similar 'competition between the first and the last syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Noun plural suffix -tëjk receives primary stress (128); diminutive -u'unk (historically 'child') does not, which distinguishes diminutive suffixation from noun 'child' in composition (129-130); clitics (=a INT, =ëk hearsay) never stressed (131). Convergent statements for the other varieties under this glottocode: Tlahuitoltepec proper (Lyon 1980:33) 'la sílaba tónica de la palabra es la sílaba del radical' except certain always-tonic verbal suffixes; Tamazulápam (Santiago Martínez 2015:53-58) final/iambic in monomorphemic words with tonic ('heavy') vs atonic ('light') suffix classes.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the morphological stem (root + derivation/compounding), right edge; inflectional suffixes and enclitics lie outside it, so verb forms surface with penult/antepenult word-level stress. Examples are citation forms of single words; no phrase-level conditioning described.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Ayutla variety (San Pedro y San Pablo Ayutla, 'Tukyo'm Ayuujk'), which Glottolog files under tlah1239 (South Highland Mixe, ISO mxp; no separate glottocode). The eponymous Santa María Tlahuitoltepec variety is described first-hand by Lyon 1980 (ALIM 8) p.33, saved and read: accent non-contrastive, 'la sílaba tónica de la palabra es la sílaba del radical' except certain always-tonic verbal suffixes — the same root/stem-based rule (note Lyon's p.34 footnote that his accent exposition is adapted from Crawford's Totontepec framework). Tamazulápam (Santiago Martínez 2015 §2.7, also under tlah1239) is likewise final/iambic with tonic vs atonic suffix classes. 'Yacochi Tlahuitoltepec' (Martínez García 2010, penult stress, 9 vowels) is a Totontepec-type North Highland variety spoken inside Tlahuitoltepec municipality and should not be conflated with tlah1239.

Except in verbs, the stress is word final. In verbs, on the other hand, the last syllable of the verb stem is stressed. The verb stem is defined as what is left after the inflectional morphology is removed.' [fn 12]; p. 80 'In phonetic terms, the stress is usually realized as both higher pitch and greater intensity. In phonological terms, stress does not have any contrastive function, i.e. there are no minimal pairs..'; p. 80 'In compounds, the last syllable of the second root takes the stress, as illustrated in (124).'; p. 81 'Prefixes…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the same work and the same passage as the sole existing_statement (reading 'morphologically determined', §3.7 p. 80); the full read confirms that statement verbatim and supplies the secondary-stress and affix/clitic details (pp. 81-83) and the non-contrastiveness statement. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field, so this work fills it rather than contradicting it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the last syllable of the word in all word classes except verbs; in verbs it is on the last syllable of the verb stem (root plus derivation, minus inflectional suffixes such as -ë INV, -të PL, -p INDEP, which never take stress). Prefixes and clitics never bear stress; in compounds the last syllable of the second root is stressed; the noun plural suffix -tëjk does take stress, the diminutive -u'unk does not. Stress is non-contrastive (no minimal pairs) and is realized by higher pitch and greater intensity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Trisyllabic words: first syllable takes secondary stress, last keeps primary (e.g. [ˌnɨ.tɨ.ɡɨːk] 'third'); if the third syllable is a suffix, primary stress is on the second syllable and there is no secondary stress ([a.mɨh.kɨp]). With two or three suffixes after a verb stem, the stem-final syllable has primary stress and the word-final syllable secondary stress ([tɨh.kɨ.ˌdɨp] 'they enter', [tɨh.kɨ.ɲɨ.ˌdɨp]). Footnote 13: in mëjä'äy-tëjk [mɨ.ˌhʌʌ.dʲɨʰk] the penultimate bears secondary stress next to the primary, called 'somehow anomalous'. Author notes other Mixe languages seem to show 'a competition between the first and the last syllable' (p. 83).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs (stem-final rather than word-final); noun plural suffix -tëjk is stressed while diminutive -u'unk is not (stress distinguishes affixation from compounding, ex. 130); clitics (=a INT, =ëk hearsay) never stressed even word-finally; monosyllables trivially stressed.
new_statements.identity_note: Romero-Méndez 2008 describes Ayutla Mixe (Tukyo'm Ayuujk, San Pedro y San Pablo Ayutla), which he treats as one of the dialects of South Highland Mixe following Wichmann (1995a), alongside Tlahuitoltepec, Tamazulapam, Tepuxtepec, Tepantlali and Mixistlán (pp. 7-9 region). Glottolog files it under the languoid tlah1239 'Tlahuitoltepec Mixe' (ISO mxp); the catalog name 'Ayutla Mixe' therefore refers to this Ayutla variety, not Tlahuitoltepec proper.

sources.note: p.53-54 (Tamazulápam variety): 'El acento en MTM no es contrastivo.. En palabras monomorfémicas el acento siempre en yámbico, es decir, en todo momento cae en la última sílaba'; prefixes never stressed; verbs/nouns: 'heavy' (tonic) suffixes take final stress, 'light' (atonic) suffixes are invisible so the root keeps stress (can yield antepenult); calls MTM 'lengua de acento yámbico y morfológico'; notes Lyon 1980 saw tonic/atonic suffixes in Tlahuitoltepec; contrasts with penult (trochaic) stress in Totontepec/Metepec/Yacochi.
